items.title: Jack DeJohnette interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 7, 2025
items.q: Bitches Brew was basically kind of a jam session with... different players would solo on top of that... Miles let the tapes roll

ctx.x: And there’s a quote in here from you, “I got around so well on Miles’ music because I like the unexpected.” Was “Bitches Brew” an unexpected situation for you or had you been sort of set up for that?

Yeah I was set up and prepared. I’m from Chicago, where I played various kinds of music. So I didn’t have any biases toward all the so-called genres of music. You know “Bitches Brew” was basically kind of a jam session with — not highly arranged, but with, you know, melodic interludes in between things. And then Miles let the tapes roll and got a groove that he liked and then he would play or somebody — Bennie Maupin would play, different players would solo on top of that. And then through Teo Macero, © Fillius…
his producer, through his artistry of putting all the different tracks together to tell a story, he did that very well.

items.title: Jack DeJohnette — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I used to get these jazz records and go down to the basement and play with ... Miles Davis ... I heard that Miles Davis Quintet when George Coleman was in the group. They came through Chicago ... I remember, because they all had jackets with their names on them.

ctx.x: … So all this time, I hadn't started playing jazz yet, but I had a combo locally around my house. The drummer, [I think] his name was Johnny, he liked to mess around with cars, fixing up his car, and he played drums as a hobby and he left his drums down in my basement. This is during the time when my uncle had the jazz records. So I used to get these jazz records and go down to the basement and play with Max Roach and Clifford Brown and Charlie Parker, Mal Waldron, Jackie McLean, Art Blakey, Miles Davis and…
So you’re just working it out yourself? You didn't have anyone showing you anything?
